claims.text: The as-cast (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy has a large caloric response under applied magnetic and pressure fields.
The as-cast alloy has poor structural integrity and cracks during cyclic loading.
Adding 3–5 vol% SiC nanoparticles during melting will improve the alloy's mechanical integrity.
The SiC intervention will increase compressive strength by at least 50% relative to the untreated alloy.
The SiC intervention will retain a caloric response comparable to that of the untreated alloy.
The SiC intervention will reduce crack formation under cyclic mechanical and field conditions.
Controlled melting and annealing can prevent adverse reactions or decomposition of the SiC addition.
Melting at approximately 1500 °C under inert atmosphere, followed by homogenization at 1000 °C for 2 hours and controlled cooling, is an appropriate processing route.
Processing will produce a uniform dispersion of nanoscale SiC particles or controlled in-situ reaction products in the alloy matrix.
The reinforcement can be introduced without forming deleterious secondary phases.
Dispersed SiC nanoparticles will deflect and bridge cracks.
Dispersed SiC nanoparticles will improve load distribution and impede crack propagation.
SiC will remain sufficiently inert in the processed alloy to preserve the lattice instabilities responsible for the caloric transformation.
Excessively high melting temperatures or reactive atmospheres may induce unwanted reactions between SiC and alloy constituents.
SiC additions to a related CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy can form in-situ carbides, silicides, and graphite during arc melting.
SiC-derived ceramic phases in a related CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy can substantially increase strength while retaining ductility.
The intervention is expected to remain effective across the magnetic-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes that activate the caloric effect.

contradictions.description: The intervention seeks to prevent SiC decomposition and unwanted reactions, the structural mediator permits in-situ reaction products, and the mechanism relies on dispersed SiC being inert. These describe materially different reinforcement states without specifying which state is required for the predicted effect.
